title: Microfluidic Mixers for Studying Protein Folding
protocol: Fabricate Microfluidic Mixing Chips
Clean 4 inch fused silica wafers with Piranha solution at 3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 ratio heated to 130 °C.
Immerse the wafers in Piranha solution for at least 30 minutes.
Rinse the cleaned wafers with water for 5 minutes and dry.
Apply a polysilicon coating, ~1 μm thick per every intended 10 μm depth of final microfluidic channels, using LPCVD furnace.
Clean the wafers and mask using the Piranha protocol in step 1.1.
Rinse the mask with acetone, methanol, and isopropanol, then blow dry immediately.
Dehydrate the wafers on a hot plate at 150 °C for ~10 minutes or in a 120 °C oven for at least 120 min (overnight preferably).
Expose warm wafers to HMDS vapor for 5 minutes.
Spin coat the wafers with a ~900 nm thick layer of AZ5214 photoresist and soft bake at 90 °C for 1 minute or in an oven at 110 °C for 30 min.
Align the mask and make a hard and vacuum contact.
Expose to UV light for several seconds (total energy: ~103 mJ/cm²).
Develop with AZ400K developer diluted 4:1 with DI water for ~50 seconds while gently agitating.
Rinse with water for 2 minutes.
Inspect features with microscope.
If features are poorly resolved, strip the photoresist and start again from step 1.2.
Hard bake at 115 °C for 2 minutes directly on a hotplate.
Descum wafers with Asher or O2 plasma for 2.5 minutes at 100 W RF power.
Etch the polysilicon layer through to the fused silica below using a DRIE etcher.
Strip remaining photoresist with PRS2000 resist stripper at 75 °C for 10 minutes.
Rinse and dry wafers after stripping.
Measure the etch depth to ensure it is all the way through the poly coating.
Etch fused silica to a depth of ~10 μm per micron thickness of the poly coating using an oxide capable DRIE such as ULVAC NLD-6000.
Clean wafers with the Matrix Asher for 4 minutes, 100 W RF power.
Strip polysilicon with a XeF2 etcher.
Spin coat wafers with a new ~1 μm layer of photoresist to protect the channels during subsequent handling.
Drill entrance and exit holes in each chip using a computer controlled diamond-tipped drill or manually with a sandblaster.
Mount the wafer (feature-side down) on a sacrificial glass plate using Aqua Bond 55, taking care to keep the bonder free of bubbles.
Cool the drill with micro-90 cleaning solution.
Rinse the wafer with DI water using a syringe to inject water into each hole.
Soak the wafer in soapy water for an hour.
Remove photoresist and Aqua Bond with PRS 2000 at 60 °C for several hours until surface is clean.
Rinse the wafer with DI water and warm soapy water.
Rinse each hole again with a syringe, avoiding etched features.
Dry the wafer with nitrogen and in a vacuum oven set to 120 °C.
Inspect holes to ensure they are free of grit and repeat cleaning steps as necessary.
Measure the depth of the channels with either an optical or mechanical surface profiler.
Clean wafers and an equivalent number of 170 μm thick fused silica cover glasses with Piranha solution for 1-2 hours according to the procedure in 1.1.
Rinse with DI water for 5 minutes.
Treat with RCA 2 (5:1:1 DI:HCl:H2O2) solution for 10 minutes at 75 °C.
Rinse with DI water for 5 minutes.
Treat with RCA 1 (5:1:1 DI:NH4OH:H2O2) solution for 22 minutes at 75 °C.
Rinse with DI water for 5 minutes.
Place one wafer features side up on top of a stack of 3-4 cleanroom wipes.
Dry the wafer thoroughly with nitrogen gas for at least 5 minutes.
Repeat drying procedure with cover glass.
Pick up cover glass by the edge.
Invert cover glass such that the polished side is face down held over the wafer.
Align flat edges of wafer and cover glass.
Carefully drop the cover glass onto the wafer and allow it to settle.
Nudge horizontally only to adjust alignment.
Push down with one finger on the center of the wafer.
Apply additional pressure at other positions around the wafer if necessary.
Place the sealed wafers in a high temperature oven set to ramp from room temp to 800 °C over 3 hours.
Ramp from 800 - 1100 °C over another 1.2 hours.
Hold at 1100 °C for 2 hours.
Ramp down to room temperature over another 1.5 hours.
Dice with a wafer dicing saw into individual chips.
Prepare the manifold for holding the mixing chip using plastic or aluminum material.
Coat solution reservoirs with parylene if using an aluminum manifold.
Mount thermoelectric devices on the sides of the manifold for temperature control.
Use an electronic controller to regulate the temperature throughout the system.
Mate the microfluidic chip to the manifold using small o-rings.
Secure the microfluidic chip in place with a retaining ring allowing optical viewing.
Ensure o-ring grooves are shallow enough to avoid excessive pressure on the chip.
Mount the chip and add solutions to the center and side reservoirs carefully.
Release any bubbles trapped at the bottom of the wells before proceeding.
Control flow through the system using air pressure applied above the solution wells.
Connect the pressure manifold to computer-controlled pressure transducers for control.
Place manifold on an inverted microscope and examine mixing region with the eyepiece or camera output.
Use an incandescent flashlight placed on top of the manifold to provide light.
Insert a dye or high index of refraction solution in the center channel to view the jet.
Start with the side channel pressure at 0 PSI and slowly increase to equal pressure as needed.
Apply pressure or vacuum to the exit channel with a syringe if a visible clog appears.
Clean the chip by soaking it in Pirhana solution overnight if protein or other organic material causes clogs.
Bring a collimated laser beam into a research-grade microscope using a dichroic mirror either inside or just outside the microscope.
Align the laser so that the focus can be seen in the eyepiece or camera near the mixing region.
Collect fluorescence from the protein in the mixer by the objective and send it through the dichroic mirror.
Focus the collected fluorescence with a lens to a pinhole and image it on a photon counter.
Scan the chip using a piezoelectric scanner in x and y to image the mixing region (typical step size is 2 μm).
Choose a position on the jet and scan in x and z to find the focus at the center of the channel vertically.
Scan horizontally within the exit channel (typical step size is 0.2 μm across the jet, 2 μm along the jet) in 100 μm increments along the jet, observing for approximately 1 ms per position.
Move the microscope stage by 80-90 μm along the jet to capture later times.
Collect data in 100 μm increments along a 500 μm-long exit channel.
Examine overlapping data from multiple views to eliminate signal offsets due to focus changes.
Confirm spectroscopic changes by comparing data collected at different flow rates.
